slides.text: Paris, 1700s. The Holy Innocents cemetery was a mound packed with centuries of dead. Cellar walls next to it started to collapse.
The answer was underneath the city: miles of old limestone quarries.
From 1786, covered wagons carried the bones through the streets at night. Procession after procession.
It took decades. In the end, the remains of more than six million Parisians were stacked down here.
Over the entrance, a warning: 'Stop! Here is the empire of Death.'
1793. Philibert Aspairt, a hospital doorkeeper, went down a staircase into the quarries. He never came back up.
His body was found 11 years later, in 1804. He was buried right where he lay. His tomb is still down there.
Today you can tour a small part of it. The rest, hundreds of kilometres of tunnels, is off-limits.
